results.claim: The recorded target is dimensionally inconsistent: literal ISO A9-in-A1 has optimum 258, so it is neither 518 nor 519.
results.proof_sketch: The authorized source gives A1 dimensions 594×841, A9 dimensions 37×52, and A10 dimensions 26×37. Its Table 1 places the A1/A9 bound at 258–259 and the A1/A10 bound at 518–519. Numerically, the container area is 594·841=499554, whereas an A9 has area 37·52=1924; already 260·1924=500240>499554, so 518 and 519 cannot describe literal A9-in-A1. The matching construction and upper certificate in the next claim prove the sharper value 258.

results.claim: OPT(594,841,52,37)=258, with an explicit placement and a periodic upper-bound certificate.
results.proof_sketch:
For the lower bound, split the width as 37+37+260+260. In each 37-wide strip stack sixteen 37×52 rectangles. In each 260-wide strip place four 52-high rows of seven 37×52 rectangles, then seventeen 37-high rows of five 52×37 rectangles. The wide strips use height 4·52+17·37=837 and contain 28+85=113 rectangles each, giving 2·16+2·113=258 total.

For the upper bound, first reduce any real-coordinate packing to an integer-coordinate one by flooring every lower-left coordinate. Containment is preserved because all dimensions are integers. For every disjoint pair, at least one separating inequality, such as x_i+w_i≤x_j, holds; flooring preserves it because floor(x_i)+w_i=floor(x_i+w_i)≤floor(x_j). Thus all pairwise disjointness is preserved.

On the integer unit-cell grid, mark columns with residues {2,9,16,24,31} modulo 37 and rows with residues {5,12,19,27,34}; give each marked intersection weight 1/35. Every 37-cell interval has five marks. The cyclic gaps are 7,7,8,7,8, whose adjacent sums are at most 15, so every 15-cell interval has at least two marks and every 52-cell interval has at least seven. Hence either A9 orientation covers at least 5·7=35 marked cells. The container has 80 marked columns and 113 marked rows, so its total weight is 9040/35=258+2/7<259. Every packing therefore has at most 258 rectangles.

results.claim: If the intended 518/519 instance is ISO A10-in-A1, its exact optimum is 518.
results.proof_sketch:
For the lower bound, split the width as 74+520. The 74-wide strip contains 32 rows of two 37×26 rectangles, giving 64. In the 520-wide strip, fifteen 37-high rows contain twenty 26×37 rectangles each, and eleven 26-high rows contain fourteen 37×26 rectangles each. The height is 15·37+11·26=841 and this strip contains 300+154=454 rectangles, for 518 total.

For the upper bound, use the same flooring reduction. Mark both axes at residues R={2,6,10,14,17,21,25,28,32,36} modulo 37 and give marked intersections weight 1/70. Every 37-cell interval has ten marks. The cyclic gaps are 4,4,4,3,4,4,3,4,4,3; every three consecutive gaps sum to at least 11, so an 11-cell interval contains at most three marks. Its complementary 26-cell interval therefore contains at least seven. Thus either A10 orientation covers at least 7·10=70 marked cells. There are 160 marked columns and 227 marked rows, and the total weight is 36320/70=518+6/7<519. Hence at most 518 fit, matching the construction.

final_writeup:
The answer to the literal target is neither 518 nor 519: exactly 258 ISO A9 sheets fit in one ISO A1 sheet. The source’s 518–519 alternatives belong to A10-in-A1, whose optimum is 518.

Let the A1 container be C=[0,594]×[0,841]. An A9 is 37×52, with rotation allowed. A 258-packing is given by these families:

1. For s∈{0,1} and k=0,…,15, place [37s,37(s+1)]×[52k,52(k+1)].
2. For X∈{74,334}, k=0,…,3, and c=0,…,6, place [X+37c,X+37(c+1)]×[52k,52(k+1)].
3. For the same X, k=0,…,16, and c=0,…,4, place [X+52c,X+52(c+1)]×[208+37k,208+37(k+1)].

These families contain 32, 56, and 170 rectangles. Their disjoint strip-and-band structure proves non-overlap; their maximum coordinates are x=594 and y=837.

It remains to prove optimality at the requested real-coordinate packing strength. Given any real-coordinate packing, floor both coordinates of every lower-left corner. Containment remains valid because the rectangle and container dimensions are integers. For each pair of rectangles, interior-disjointness supplies a separating inequality along at least one axis. If, for example, x_i+w_i≤x_j, then floor(x_i)+w_i=floor(x_i+w_i)≤floor(x_j), so that separation survives flooring. The other three possible inequalities are identical. Thus it suffices to bound integer-coordinate packings.

Mark unit-grid columns whose residues modulo 37 are {2,9,16,24,31} and rows whose residues are {5,12,19,27,34}. Assign weight 1/35 at marked intersections and zero elsewhere. Every 37-cell interval contains five marks, and every 52-cell interval contains at least seven, so every A9 rectangle has weight at least one. The container contains 80 marked columns and 113 marked rows, hence total weight 80·113/35=258+2/7. Since packing cardinality is integral, it is at most 258. Together with the construction, this proves OPT(594,841,52,37)=258.

For completeness, the evident corrected question uses A10 dimensions 26×37. Split C into widths 74 and 520. Pack the first strip with 32 rows of two 37×26 rectangles. Pack the second with fifteen rows of twenty 26×37 rectangles and eleven rows of fourteen 37×26 rectangles. This gives 64+300+154=518.

For its upper bound, mark both axes at residues {2,6,10,14,17,21,25,28,32,36} modulo 37 and assign marked intersections weight 1/70. Every 37-cell interval has ten marks and every 26-cell interval at least seven, so each A10 receives weight at least one. The total weight is 160·227/70=518+6/7<519. Therefore the corrected A10-in-A1 optimum is 518.

Accordingly, the literal false dichotomy and its evident intended interpretation are both completely resolved.
